cognate: ON garðr ~ Ved. gṛhá- (same root *gʰerdʰ-/*gʰordʰo- vs *gʰr̥dʰó-; the lexicon carries them under two ids, pie-lex-ghordhos and pie-lex-ghrdhos); faðir ~ pitṛ́-, móðir ~ mātṛ́-, bróðir ~ bhrā́tṛ-, all genitives
drift_or_renewal: garðr has drifted from 'house' toward 'fenced homestead/farm' in Norse, Ved. gṛhá 'house'; otherwise none
shared_syntax: locative/prepositional 'in the house' + kin genitive, with the house-noun stated once and two further kin genitives coordinated elliptically: ON i faður garðe eða moðor eða broðor (AM-302; AM-56 w926/w929 have faður ... broðor) ~ AV mātuḥ ... gṛhe atha u bhrātuḥ atha u pituḥ
context: Both concern an unmarried daughter whose status is defined by her remaining in the house of her natal guardians (father, mother, brother): the Norwegian inheritance law treats a daughter who is 'legin' (has lain with a man) while in father's/mother's/brother's homestead; AVŚ 1.14 (= AVP 1.15) is a spell binding a girl to remain unmarried (kulapā) in mother's, brother's and father's house. AM-56 w854 gives the same guardian triad (faðer, broðer, moðer) as the giftingarmaðr who disposes of her marriage. Epic Sanskrit uses pitur gṛhe repeatedly of a daughter's natal home; Gothic in garda attins (John 14:2, recalled). 'Father's house' alone is generic; what lifts this is the cognate house-word plus the same three-guardian triad in elliptic coordination, in the same social context. The triad is natural in any patrilocal society, the Norse text is a 13th-c. Christian-era law, and word orders differ; chance co-formation from inherited lexicon cannot be excluded.
phrase: *ph₂tros gʰordʰo- 'in the father's (mother's, brother's) house' of the unmarried daughter

search_lead.cognate: ON ljós 'light' (*lewk-s-) ~ Lat. lūmen (*lewk-smn̥), same root *lewk-
search_lead.argument: ON law: a child begotten but not yet born (geteð oc æigi fǿtt) inherits 'ef þæt kǫmr lifí i líos' (if it comes alive into the light) and is baptised; Lucretius repeatedly expresses birth as coming (alive) 'in luminis oras'. Birth = coming into the light with a *lewk- noun and a motion verb in both; Homer's πρὸ φόωσδε (Il. 16.188, of birth) gives the figure in Greek with another root. Universal metaphor, Lucretius is Ennian/epic diction; worth a reviewer's look only as figure + root.

search_lead.cognate: ON bani 'death, slaying' (*gʷʰonō) ~ Skt hata- 'slain' (*gʷʰn̥tó-), root *gʷʰen-; 'victory' not cognate (sigr vs ji-)
search_lead.argument: Harald fights so hard that 'anat tvegia scyldi hann fa sigr eða bana' (either victory or death); MBh has the warrior's alternative 'slain, or victorious'. Same disjunctive figure, one root shared. 'Victory or death' is a near-universal battle topos, so weak.
